title: Binary Search Tree
html:
A binary search tree keeps keys in order: smaller keys to the left, larger to the right, at every node. That one rule turns search, insert, delete, floor and ceiling into a single walk down one path — O(log n) when the tree is balanced — and makes an inorder traversal print the keys sorted.

Binary search tree (BST) — a binary tree in which, for every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller than the node's key and all keys in its right subtree are greater. Keys are usually assumed distinct. Like a linked list it is a linked data structure: nodes connected by pointers, no fixed capacity.

Check the invariant at any node: left of 20 are 15 12 18 7 (all smaller), right are 30 40 35 50 80 (all larger). Left of 40 is 35, right is 50 80. It holds for the whole subtree, not just the two children — a tree where 35 sat under 15 would have every child in order and still be wrong.

Watch out

The invariant is left subtree < node < right subtree, not left child < node < right child. A node's right child may have a left child, and that grandchild must still be greater than the node — e.g. 35 is a left child of 40 but greater than 30.

Why a BST: comparison with other structures

A BST is the structure for data that must stay sorted while it changes. Arrays are fast at one thing and slow at the other; a hash table is fastest for exact lookups but knows nothing about order.

OperationUnsorted arraySorted arrayLinked listBST (balanced)Hash table
SearchO(n)O(log n)O(n)O(log n)O(1) average
InsertO(1)O(n)O(1)O(log n)O(1) average
DeleteO(n)O(n)O(n)O(log n)O(1) average
Find closest (floor / ceiling)O(n)O(log n)O(n)O(log n)O(n)
Sorted traversalO(n log n)O(n)O(n log n)O(n)O(n log n)

Every BST operation walks one root-to-leaf path, so it costs O(h) where h is the height. The balanced column assumes h = O(log n); the self-balancing section shows how libraries guarantee it. Those libraries are the ready-made BSTs you should normally use:

LanguageOrdered setOrdered mapImplementation
C++std::set, std::multisetstd::map, std::multimapred-black tree
JavaTreeSetTreeMapred-black tree
Python— (use sortedcontainers.SortedList, or bisect on a list)—no BST in the standard library
JavaScript——none built in — implement one or use a library

Operations and their cost

OperationHowTime
search(k)Go left if k is smaller, right if larger, stop on match or nullO(h)
insert(k)Search for k; attach a new leaf where the search fell offO(h)
delete(k)Search, then one of three cases (leaf, one child, two children)O(h)
min() / max()Follow left / right pointers to the endO(h)
floor(k) / ceil(k)Search, remembering the last candidate on the way downO(h)
inorder()Left, node, right — visits keys in sorted orderO(n)

h is ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ for a perfectly balanced tree and n for a degenerate one, so the same code runs in O(log n) or O(n) depending only on the shape.

Insert

Example

Input: insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7 into an empty tree
Output: the sample BST; inorder 7 12 15 18 20 30 35 40 50 80
Input: then insert 60
Output: 60 becomes the left child of 80

Idea

Search for the key. If you find it, do nothing (no duplicates). If you fall off the tree at a null pointer, that is exactly where the key belongs: create a leaf there. The recursive version returns the (possibly new) root of each subtree so the parent can re-attach it — root.left = insert(root.left, key) — which handles the empty-tree case for free.

Time O(h)Space O(h) recursion stack

Iterative insert avoids the recursion stack: walk down with a parent pointer until curr is null, then hang the new node on the correct side of parent. Same O(h) time, O(1) extra space.

Time O(h)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Inserting keys that arrive already sorted (1, 2, 3, 4, …) builds a right-skewed chain of height n: every later operation is O(n). Shuffle the input, or use a self-balancing tree.

Key point

Inorder traversal of a BST always prints the keys in ascending order — so build a BST, traverse inorder is a sorting algorithm (tree sort), O(n log n) when the tree stays balanced.

Search

Example

Input: the sample BST, key = 7
Output: true
Input: key = 25
Output: false

Idea

Compare the key with the current node. Equal — found. Smaller — the key can only be in the left subtree, so go left. Larger — go right. Reaching null means the key is absent. Each step discards an entire subtree, which is why it is O(h) and not O(n): binary search on a tree.

Time O(h)Space O(h) recursive, O(1) iterative
Key point

The recursion here is a tail call — nothing happens after it returns — which is why the iterative version is a trivial rewrite and the one to prefer in production code.

Delete

Example

Input: the sample BST, delete 7 (a leaf)
Output: inorder 12 15 18 20 30 35 40 50 80
Input: delete 30 (one child)
Output: 40 takes its place: 12 15 18 20 35 40 50 80
Input: delete 20 (two children)
Output: replaced by its inorder successor 35: 12 15 18 35 40 50 80

Idea

Search for the key, then fix the hole it leaves. A leaf can simply go. A node with one child is replaced by that child. A node with two children cannot be unlinked without breaking the shape — instead copy the inorder successor (the smallest key of the right subtree, found by walking left from right) into the node and delete the successor from the right subtree; the successor has no left child, so that second deletion is always case 1 or 2.

1
Find the node
Recurse left or right as in search; root.left = delete(root.left, key) re-attaches whatever comes back.
2
Leaf, or one child
Return the child (or null) to the parent — the node is bypassed.
3
Two children
Find succ = min(root.right), copy succ.key into root, then root.right = delete(root.right, succ.key).
Time O(h)Space O(h)
Pitfall

In case 3 you may equally use the inorder predecessor (max of the left subtree). What you must not do is move the successor node without removing it from where it was, or forget to re-attach the result of the recursive delete — the classic bug is delete_key(root.right, succ.key) without the root.right =.

Key point

Why O(h): the search is one path down, and the successor walk plus its deletion continue down the same path (successor is in the right subtree, and deleting it is another walk down). Total work is at most twice the height.

Floor in a BST

Example

Input: the sample BST, x = 14
Output: 12 (the largest key ≤ 14)
Input: x = 1
Output: none (every key is larger)
Input: x = 20
Output: 20
Input: x = 100
Output: 80

Floor of x — the largest key in the tree that is ≤ x. Ceiling is the smallest key ≥ x. Together they answer what is closest to x — something a hash table cannot do.

Idea

Walk down as in search, keeping the best candidate seen so far. At a node with key < x the node is a candidate — remember it, then go right to look for something closer to x. At a node with key > x it cannot be the floor, go left. On an exact match the answer is the node itself. When the walk hits null, the remembered candidate is the floor.

1
key == x
Return this node — nothing can be closer.
2
key > x
Too big; the floor must be in the left subtree: root = root.left.
3
key < x
A valid candidate; a larger one may exist to the right: res = root; root = root.right.
Time O(h)Space O(1)

Ceiling in a BST

Example

Input: the sample BST, x = 21
Output: 30 (the smallest key ≥ 21)
Input: x = 5
Output: 7
Input: x = 7
Output: 7
Input: x = 81
Output: none

Idea

The mirror image of floor. A key > x is a candidate — remember it and go left for something closer; a key < x is useless, go right; an exact match is the answer.

1
key == x
Return this node.
2
key < x
Too small; the ceiling must be on the right: root = root.right.
3
key > x
A valid candidate; a smaller one may exist to the left: res = root; root = root.left.
Time O(h)Space O(1)
Key point

Floor and ceiling in a sorted array are binary search (bisect_right(a, x) - 1 and bisect_left(a, x) in Python). The BST versions are the same idea on a structure that also supports O(log n) insert and delete — which is exactly what floor / ceiling in a stream needs.

Self-balancing BSTs: why and how

The same set of keys can make BSTs of very different heights — it depends only on the insertion order. The operations above are O(h), so the whole point of balancing is to keep h = O(log n) no matter what order the keys arrive in.

If all keys were known in advance we could build the perfectly balanced tree directly (insert the middle of the sorted keys, then recurse on each half). With random insertions and deletions we cannot — so a self-balancing tree restructures itself after every insert or delete that makes it lopsided.

The restructuring tool is the rotation: a local change of two or three pointers that moves a subtree one level up on one side and one level down on the other without breaking the BST order — the inorder sequence T1 y T2 x T3 is the same before and after.

RotationPointer changesEffect
Right rotation at xy = x.left; x.left = y.right; y.right = x; P now points at yLeft subtree gets one level shorter, right subtree one level taller
Left rotation at yx = y.right; y.right = x.left; x.left = y; P now points at xThe mirror image

The two famous self-balancing BSTs differ only in what counts as balanced and therefore in when they rotate: the AVL tree (strict, by height) and the red-black tree (looser, by colouring).

AVL tree

AVL tree — a BST in which, for every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. The balance factor bf = height(left) − height(right) is therefore always −1, 0 or +1; a node with |bf| > 1 is unbalanced and must be rotated.

Named after Adelson-Velsky and Landis (1962). The height condition guarantees h ≤ 1.44 log₂ n, so every operation is O(log n). Each node stores its height so the balance factor is O(1) to compute.

1
Normal BST insert
Walk down and attach the new leaf as usual.
2
Walk back up updating heights
The recursion returns through every ancestor of the new node; recompute height = 1 + max(hL, hR) at each.
3
Find the first unbalanced ancestor
The lowest node with |bf| > 1. Only ancestors can be unbalanced, and fixing the lowest one fixes everything above it for an insert.
4
Rotate according to one of four cases
Decided by which grandchild subtree the new key went into.
CaseWhere the key wentFixRotations
Left-Left (LL)Left child's left subtree (bf > 1 and key < left.key)Right rotation at the unbalanced node1 (single)
Right-Right (RR)Right child's right subtree (bf < −1 and key > right.key)Left rotation at the unbalanced node1 (single)
Left-Right (LR)Left child's right subtree (bf > 1 and key > left.key)Left rotation at the left child, then right rotation at the node2 (double)
Right-Left (RL)Right child's left subtree (bf < −1 and key < right.key)Right rotation at the right child, then left rotation at the node2 (double)
Example

Input: insert 20, 15, 5
Output: root 15 — preorder 15 5 20
Input: insert 20, 15, 30, 40, 50, 12, 18, 35, 80, 7
Output: preorder 20 15 12 7 18 40 30 35 50 80, height 4 (a plain BST has height 5)

Time O(log n) per insert — one path down plus at most two rotationsSpace O(log n) recursion stack
Key point

Why at most two rotations: after an insert, fixing the lowest unbalanced node restores that subtree to its original height, so no ancestor can still be unbalanced. Deletion is different — a rotation may shorten the subtree, so the fix can cascade up the whole path, O(log n) rotations.

Pitfall

The notes wrote the AVL condition as |lh − rh| < 1; it is |lh − rh| ≤ 1. With < 1 only perfect trees would qualify and no tree with n = 2 nodes could exist.

Red-black tree

Red-black tree — a BST in which every node carries one extra bit — a colour, red or black — and four rules on the colours keep the longest root-to-leaf path at most twice as long as the shortest. This guarantees h ≤ 2 log₂(n + 1), so all operations are O(log n).

  1. Every node is either red or black.
  2. The root is always black.
  3. No two consecutive reds: a red node has only black children (a red node's parent is black).
  4. Every path from a node down to its descendant null leaves has the same number of black nodes (the black height).

Why the rules bound the height. Rule 4 says every path has the same number b of black nodes; rule 3 says reds cannot be adjacent, so a path has at most b reds squeezed between its blacks. The shortest possible path is all black (b nodes); the longest alternates (2b nodes). Hence no path is more than twice as long as any other — the statement at the end of the notes — and since a tree with b blacks on every path has at least 2^b − 1 nodes, b ≤ log₂(n + 1) and h ≤ 2 log₂(n + 1).

Insertion colours the new node red (that never breaks rule 4), then fixes any red-red violation by recolouring and at most two rotations. Deletion is more involved but also needs at most three rotations. The code is long and rarely asked in interviews; the properties and the comparison below are.

AVL treeRed-black tree
Balance rule|hL − hR| ≤ 1 at every node (strict)Colour rules; longest path ≤ 2 × shortest (loose)
Height bound≤ 1.44 log₂ n — shorter≤ 2 log₂ n — a bit taller
SearchFaster (shorter tree)Slightly slower
Insert≤ 2 rotations, but more frequent rebalancing≤ 2 rotations, mostly just recolouring
DeleteUp to O(log n) rotations≤ 3 rotations
Extra data per nodeHeight (an int) or balance factor1 bit (the colour)
Best forLookup-heavy data that changes rarely (databases, dictionaries)Frequent inserts/deletes
Used inSome database indexes, Windows kernelstd::map/set, Java TreeMap/TreeSet, Linux scheduler (CFS) and memory manager

Applications of a BST

Sorted dynamic data

Keep a stream of keys sorted while they keep arriving: inorder is always sorted, insert/delete stay O(log n) — std::set, TreeMap.

Double-ended priority queue

A heap gives only the min or the max; a BST gives both (leftmost and rightmost) plus delete-any in O(log n).

Floor, ceiling, nearest in a stream

What is the largest value ≤ x among the values seen so far? — floor/ceiling on a self-balancing BST.

Count smaller / greater in a stream

Augment each node with the size of its subtree; rank queries then take one walk down, O(log n).

Range queries

All keys in [lo, hi]: go down to lo, then inorder until hi — O(h + k) for k results.

Language libraries

C++ map/set/multimap/multiset, Java TreeMap/TreeSet are red-black trees; database B-trees are the same idea with many keys per node.

Interview Q&A

How do you check whether a binary tree is a BST?

Not by comparing each node with its two children — that misses a grandchild on the wrong side. Either do an inorder traversal and check that the sequence is strictly increasing, or pass a valid range (lo, hi) down the recursion: the left child must be in (lo, node.key), the right in (node.key, hi). Both are O(n).

What is the worst-case complexity of search in a BST, and how do you avoid it?

O(n), when the tree is skewed (keys inserted in sorted order make a linked list). Avoid it with a self-balancing tree — AVL or red-black — which guarantees h = O(log n) by rotating after inserts and deletes.

How do you delete a node that has two children?

Replace its key with the inorder successor (the minimum of the right subtree) or the inorder predecessor (maximum of the left), then delete that successor from the subtree it came from. The successor has at most one child, so the second deletion is the easy case. Total O(h).

How do you find the kth smallest element in a BST?

An inorder traversal visits keys in ascending order, so stop at the kth visited node — O(h + k). If the query is frequent, store the subtree size in each node: at a node with s keys in its left subtree, go left if k ≤ s, return the node if k = s + 1, else go right with k − s − 1. That is O(h).

AVL or red-black — which would you choose?

AVL for lookup-heavy workloads: its stricter balance keeps the tree shorter. Red-black for insert/delete-heavy workloads: fewer rotations per update and only one bit of extra storage. Most standard libraries (std::map, TreeMap) chose red-black.

How do a BST and a hash table compare?

A hash table gives O(1) average search/insert/delete but has no notion of order: no min/max, floor/ceiling, sorted traversal or range queries. A balanced BST gives all of those in O(log n) and has no worst-case collisions. Use a hash table for pure key lookups, a BST when order matters.
